text: By one account, about 2,000 years ago in what is now southern Zimbabwe, San peoples met herders from East Africa.
From these meetings came the Khoekhoe, who spread south with their sheep and later their cattle, across the Orange River.
src: 400 BCE–100 CE: By Mellet’s account a proto-Khoe people emerges in southern Zimbabwe as San peoples meet herders from East Africa
with their sheep and later cattle, Khoekhoe herders spread south to the Cape / After 1000 CE: Widespread Khoekhoe settlements and large herds appear south of the Orange River

text: For centuries they moved from place to place with their herds of sheep, goats and cattle.
Groups in the west called themselves ǀAwakhoen and those in the south ǀKx’abakhoena, both meaning “Red People”.
src: They were traditionally nomadic pastoralists / Sheep, goats and cattle grazed in fertile valleys
Groups to the west called themselves ǀAwakhoen, and those of the south and the Eastern Cape ǀKx’abakhoena, both meaning “Red People”

text: In 1510, Khoekhoe riding on oxen beat a Portuguese party at Salt River and killed its leader.
Later, ships stopping in Table Bay traded tobacco, copper and iron with them for fresh meat.
src: In 1510 ox-mounted ǃUriǁ’aekua defeated the party of Francisco de Almeida at the Battle of Salt River, killing him and fifty of his men
Later in the century ships of many nations stopped in Table Bay and traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoekhoe clans for fresh meat

text: Dutch settlers took their grazing land for farms, and smallpox, a disease brought by Europeans, killed many.
In 1829 some Khoekhoe were given land of their own at Kat River, on the Cape’s eastern frontier.
src: Smallpox brought through European contact killed many / the Dutch East India Company began to enclose their grazing land for farms
1829: The Kat River Settlement gives Khoekhoe land of their own near the eastern frontier of the Cape Colony

text: In a war with German forces from 1904 to 1907, more than half of the Nama people may have died.
Later, under apartheid, unfair laws in South Africa kept people apart by race and forced many families from their homes.
src: in German South-West Africa from 1904 to 1907 over 10,000 Nama, more than half the people, may have died
Under apartheid some Khoekhoe were classified as “Coloured” / They faced discrimination and segregation, and forced removals under the Group Areas Act broke up families and communities

text: Today the Nama, Damara, Griqua and Orana nations live on, and many work to bring back their culture and land.
In the Richtersveld, a World Heritage Site, herders still move their animals from pasture to pasture, as in the past.
src: The Nama, Damara, Griqua and Orana nations endure / Since then Khoekhoe activists have worked to restore their culture and their ties to the land
In the Richtersveld, inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in recognition of Khoe-speaking culture, the transhumant herding of the past still continues
